title: Ship a Vue 3 support workspace
outcome: Connect URL state, reusable components, async data, editing, tests, and measured UX in one small feature.
benefits: Turns separate concepts into a feature you can explain and change.
drawbacks: The capstone requires hands-on work beyond reading.
version: Modern JavaScript / TypeScript · Vue 3.5 where applicable · browser APIs
cue: One feature. Several boundaries. Observable promises.

trace.title: URL and user intent
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

Build one vertical feature rather than a gallery of disconnected examples.

A support workspace should open directly from a URL, load an allowed ticket list, filter it, open a ticket, edit its title, and preserve edits after a failed save.

Use a small boundary map: router owns context, an API adapter validates responses, a composable owns request lifetime, components render accessible states, and the server owns permission and concurrency rules.

Add a store only for state that really crosses component ownership boundaries.

Completion is a demonstration: a happy path, a denied request, a failed save, a reverse-order request race, a keyboard path, and a large-data profile.

Explain which evidence came from pure tests, component tests, and a browser.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Follow a search from URL to accepted rows. Follow an edit from input to versioned request to reconciled response.

Follow a failed save back to a preserved draft. Finally trace an old request that arrives after navigation and prove it has no ownership.

Add one production-style change: a new optional status from the server. Decide how older clients render it.

A strict parser can reject unexpected data; a tolerant adapter can preserve unknown states. Choose deliberately.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail: A feature can pass isolated tests while its router, API, and component contracts disagree. A polished happy path can still lose drafts or hide denied writes.
